newsitem.title: USA: Alaska ferry suit to target Canadian government.
newsitem.headline: Alaska ferry suit to target Canadian government.

text.p: A lawsuit seeking to recover revenues lost in the three-day blockade of an Alaska state ferry will target Canada's government as well as the Canadian fishermen who staged the protest, a spokesman for Alaska's governor said Thursday.

"When we file next week, the state will also be naming the Canadian federal government," said Bob King, press secretary for Gov. Tony Knowles. "We feel the federal government is in part responsible. They have a responsiblity for ensuring safe passage. So we will be suing them."

The lawsuit will probably be filed Monday, King said. Alaska Marine Highway System officials were tallying up lost passenger revenues, overtime wages and economic damages stemming from the protest, an amount "estimated in the hundreds of thousands" of dollars, he said.
The blockade by hundreds of Canadian fishing boats kept the Malaspina, an Alaska state ferry, stuck in the northern British Columbia port of Prince Rupert until late Monday.
The Canadians were protesting what they said was excessive interception by Alaskans of British Columbia-spawning salmon. Alaskans deny the charge.
Alaska Attorney General Bruce Botelho plans to argue in a Vancouver court Monday for an extension to the legal injunction protecting Alaska vessels, King said.
On Wednesday, Knowles, Alaska Lt. Gov. Fran Ulmer and Washington Gov. Gary Locke were scheduled to meet in Seattle with David Anderson, fisheries minister for Canada, King said.
Knowles, Ulmer and Locke are all Democrats; Washington state is one of the parties to the expired Pacific Salmon Treaty.
Knowles also planned to travel to Prince Rupert to discuss ways to ensure future safe travel by state ferries into the port, King said.

The Canadian city estimates it has reaped a total of $72 million in economic benefits since the Alaska Marine Highway service began, but the state suspended ferry service when the blockade began and may cancel it altogether. Prince Rupert's mayor has apologized to Knowles for the protest and asked for ferry service to resume.
Gail Phillips, speaker of Alaska's House of Representatives, appeared less conciliatory.

On a public radio show Wednesday in her hometown of Homer, the Republican legislator criticized Knowles for not canceling a long-planned tour of villages along the Yukon River during the ferry crisis.

She said Knowles should have left the Yukon River, flown by Alaska National Guard helicopter to the surrounded Malaspina, taken charge at the vessel's helm and rammed the ferry through the ring of Canadian fishing boats. Phillips is considered a possible challenger for Knowles' seat in 1998.

"With all due respect to the speaker, such an action would be highly irresponsible. It's one thing to want to live out your Walter Mitty fantasies, but the true test of leadership is coolness under fire," he said.
